第四章 —— 穷人版“自在极意功”

在我那间临时搭出来、堪称穷人版“臭鼬工厂”的实验室里折腾了一整天，试图像街头贩子熬“神秘糖浆”那样，研发一种能提升我红酒销量的专属混合饮料——虽然说实话，我现在基本只是在发明越来越离谱的“简单糖浆”——结果我突然想到一个……姑且称之为“破格”的类比。

我一边“练习脱口秀”，一边说：

我现在的臭鼬工厂状态，就像托马斯·爱迪生当年发明电灯泡一样——为了在卧室和脱衣舞俱乐部里看清楚胸部。

这句话就像一颗由蠢与天才混合而成的闪光弹，在酒吧里炸开。

为了减少爆炸半径，我尝试表现点谦虚。我补了一句：

“我只是想混口饭吃罢了。”

女调酒师立刻、面无表情地回：

“我同意。”

就是那一刻我才意识到：

我不只是被听到了。
我被共鸣了。

恭喜我自己：现代哲学家、未来对冲基金大佬、兼职“调酒师低语者”。

但当然，今晚远没这么简单。

在抛出金句之后，我立刻又被现实弹回战壕里——处理我疯癫前任的戏码，又和我爸像两个筋疲力尽的僧侣一样去做见证声明公证，好像我们在试图保存最后一卷神圣卷轴，赶在官僚主义的核弹把法院炸平之前。

画面大概是这样：

一个女孩在栗子街上尖叫。
我的太阳镜英勇牺牲。
我像情绪急救员一样努力把她塞进 Uber。
然后第二天早上：

我和我爸坐在公证办公室里，写一份文件，生怕他哪天先走一步，而书记员还在把我的核实诉状当成死海古卷一样死死卡住不让过。

如果卡夫卡写费城，这一章就是这样。

但在这一连串荒诞之中，我突然来了段“顿悟”。

来自《龙珠超》。

我突然想起悟空第一次触发“自在极意功”的那一幕——
不费力地闪避攻击。
唰、唰、唰、砰。
那是一种靠本能运转的状态，锋利到看起来轻松随意。

那就是AI。
那就是即兴。
那是一个人的思维被生存训练到极限后，不再“表演”，而是直接——行动。

边缘群体——我的群体——
所有被认为“低一等”的人、所有从毒性家庭、生硬制度、破碎体系里杀出一条路的人……
我们都懂那种感觉。

我们的自在极意功，是被逼出来的。

我们把幽默当盔甲，
把直觉当雷达，
读房间的速度比吉连出拳还快。

而真正抵达那个境界的人？

他们甚至不需要笑声。
丢一句话，空气就变了。
幽默不是为了取悦别人——那是高性能引擎的“排气声”。

这就是为什么我对那些跟女生讲话会紧张的男人说：

别学什么搭讪台词。
去学即兴喜剧。
去学如何跟一群人说话。

如果你的目标是“上床”，你已经输了。
女人闻“绝望”，就像酒保闻假身份证一样敏锐。

但如果你的目标是存在感？
砰。游戏通关。
你已经稀有了。

而说到贝吉塔和“究极我（Ultra Ego）”——
那种每挨一击就更强，但同时把自己燃烧殆尽的形态。

这就是杜波依斯说的“面具”。
舞台人格。
超自我。
一个不是靠掌声，而是靠殴打锻出来的版本。

而我终于学会什么时候要摘掉面具、停下来、做笔记。

因为即兴的快感会上瘾。
我走回家，边走边笑自己的台词，像个偷走全城市 punchline 的疯子……那种感觉太上头了。

别人看到我，都以为我嗑了什么“好东西”。
如果他们知道真相——
所谓的“好东西”，只是我的大脑终于玩得开心。

更好笑的是？

我一离开酒吧，他们一定会互相确认：

“他刚才真的说了那句？”

“说了……再给我倒一杯。”

因为安静的人也能感到那股能量。
他们回来的原因从来不是酒、不是灯光、不是音乐。

他们回来是为了**故事

24 Dic — Nochebuena: la magia que vuelve
"Hoy el mundo se llena de luz. Que también se te llene el alma."
No siempre la Nochebuena se vive como en las películas.
A veces toca trabajar,
hacer la compra con prisas,
pensar en la cena, en los regalos,
en llegar… en cumplir… en resistir.
Y aun así, la magia aparece.
En medio del cansancio,
del día largo,
de las agendas llenas.
Porque la Navidad no siempre llega envuelta en calma.
A veces llega entre bolsas, horarios, responsabilidades
y un corazón que intenta hacerlo lo mejor que puede.
Hoy, 24 de diciembre,
la magia no está en hacerlo perfecto,
sino en hacerlo con amor.
En seguir adelante,
en cuidar,
en compartir lo que se tiene, aunque sea poco tiempo, poca energía, poco descanso.
Que esta noche no te exijas más de la cuenta.
Que no te juzgues por cómo fue el día.
Que te mires con ternura y reconozcas todo lo que hiciste,
todo lo que sostuviste,
todo lo que diste.
Porque incluso así,
entre trabajo, compras, cenas y regalos,
la Navidad también estuvo ahí.
Acompañándote.
Abrazándote en silencio.
Bienvenida, Nochebuena.
Bienvenida la magia que vuelve,
aunque llegue cansada,
aunque llegue tarde,
aunque llegue de una forma distinta 🤍✨.

For the past five years, I've observed that even during the extreme cold, the East Coast has experienced a noticeable lack of precipitation. This absence of snow makes me feel less festive at this time of year and more concerned about the impact of global warming. We no longer enjoy whimsical moments like feeling a snowflake melt on your cheek while waiting for the bus stop for SEPTA, or snowball fights after school is cancelled. The extra time we used to gain for work, school, or other activities—thanks to snow days—helped us pause in our fast-paced lives, but now it is gone.
I wonder how those who grew up where snow was expected—and nearly guaranteed—feel as the year ends and another begins. It’s not so much that I miss the snow itself; I’m troubled that its absence highlights just how dry things have become, raising fears of fires reminiscent of Octavia Butler’s "Parable of the Sower." Before we can fully appreciate the season, it feels as if “’Tis the season to be worried” has become our new reality.

We judge fine artists by their finished product, but for me I have lately found myself more intrigued in how they got their, and how they developed their voice when making their art. 

It seems simple really, but constantly recreating on what you’ve already made, if your into realism adding a twist into the painting might be what your seeking. If you want to make more abstract art how are u incorporating texture, these small details are what propels a refinement in someone’s artists perspective, but most importantly on-top of that is where they come from.

For me being a Lakota artist is everything and incorporating iconography from my culture has been a big way of keeping things fresh for me and what excites me currently. I have been honoring my grandmothers life through this piece, using texture from my pallet to add depth to the Anhinga the bird of life in a lot of native culture. Using wood boards she gifted me before her passing is a way I am honoring her and continuing my creativity. 

Constantly reevaluating what we make, and how we make them is what is needed. For me it is my natural instinct and i’m excited for the new year to make more Art that both honors my own insight but my own culture.

This year, I broke and I rebuilt myself. I reimagined what my life could become. We moved states. I purchased my very own home, on my own a place my babies can truly call theirs.

I grieved more loss. I grieved being away from my land and my people. There is a sadness I carry as I move through my healing. But that sadness has awakened me to a deeper practice of gratitude.

My children are giggling and playing in the background( the soundtrack of my joy. My son is helping make the magic happen as mama’s head elf. My brothers are alive and well, and that alone is something I never take for granted. My parents are both still earthside; I hear their voices nearly every day. I have truly incredible best friends.

I’ve seen the poison of envy near me again, but it’s made me more aware, more grounded, more discerning. I’m grateful for the lessons even the painful ones. 

I love my work and my team. My body has become my home. The gym, and my trainer, have become a sanctuary for healing.

In this moment, I am humbly and completely grateful for this beautiful life.

For the past five years, I've observed that even during the extreme cold, the East Coast has experienced a noticeable lack of precipitation. This absence of snow makes me feel less festive at this time of year and more concerned about the impact of global warming. We no longer enjoy whimsical moments like feeling a snowflake melt on your cheek while waiting for the bus stop for SEPTA, or snowball fights after school is cancelled. The extra time we used to gain for work, school, or other activities—thanks to snow days—helped us pause in our fast-paced lives, but now it is gone.
I wonder how those who grew up where snow was expected—and nearly guaranteed—feel as the year ends and another begins. It’s not so much that I miss the snow itself; I’m troubled that its absence highlights just how dry things have become, raising fears of fires reminiscent of Octavia Butler’s "Parable of the Sower." Before we can fully appreciate the season, it feels as if “’Tis the season to be worried” has become our new reality.

For the past five years, I've observed that even during the extreme cold, the East Coast has experienced a noticeable lack of precipitation. This absence of snow makes me feel less festive at this time of year and more concerned about the impact of global warming. We no longer enjoy whimsical moments like feeling a snowflake melt on your cheek while waiting for the bus stop for SEPTA, or snowball fights after school is cancelled. The extra time we used to gain for work, school, or other activities—thanks to snow days—helped us pause in our fast-paced lives, but now it is gone.
I wonder how those who grew up where snow was expected—and nearly guaranteed—feel as the year ends and another begins. It’s not so much that I miss the snow itself; I’m troubled that its absence highlights just how dry things have become, raising fears of fires reminiscent of Octavia Butler’s "Parable of the Sower." Before we can fully appreciate the season, it feels as if “’Tis the season to be worried” has become our new reality.
